screens.title: Setting Up Your Unreal Engine 5 C++ Development Environment
screens.narratorSegment: Welcome. In this lesson you will build a reliable C++ development environment for Unreal Engine 5 so you can move from concept to compiled gameplay code quickly and with fewer interruptions. We begin by using the Epic Games Launcher to install Unreal Engine, then install and configure an IDE — Visual Studio on Windows or Xcode on Mac O S — with the precise C++ workloads the engine requires. Next you'll create a new C++ project and explore the Unreal Editor layout so you know where your code fits with assets and actors. Finally, we'll cover the compilation workflow, including the editor Compile button and the hot reloading mechanism that speeds iteration, and the common setup mistakes that most beginners encounter. A solid environment removes friction: you won’t lose time to missing SDKs, broken toolchains, or confusing error messages. By the end of this chapter you'll be able to create MyFirstCPPProject, open the generated solution in your IDE, compile successfully, and know how to respond when the engine needs a restart. Keep an eye out for the common-mistake checks as you follow each step.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will have four practical competencies that let you start C++ development with Unreal Engine 5. First, you will successfully install and configure Unreal Engine and the C++ IDE so the toolchain is complete and builds succeed. For example, you'll confirm Visual Studio has the 'Game development with C++' and 'Desktop development with C++' workloads. Second, you will understand why those specific workloads and SDKs matter; you'll be able to explain which components provide compilers, linkers, and Windows SDK headers, and why missing them produces build errors. Third, you will create a new C++ project and navigate the Unreal Editor's core panels so you can place actors, inspect properties, and locate your generated C++ classes. Finally, you'll perform a successful compilation, use the Editor's Compile button and hot reloading for fast iteration, and diagnose common setup and compilation problems using the Output Log and your IDE's error list. Each objective is practical: you will leave with a working project named MyFirstCPPProject and the confidence to troubleshoot the usual setup pitfalls.

screens.title: Why a Correct Development Environment Matters
screens.narratorSegment: A correct development environment is the foundation of productive Unreal Engine C++ work. Conceptually, the environment is the combination of Unreal Engine itself, the Epic Games Launcher that manages it, and the C++ toolchain your IDE provides. If any part is missing or misconfigured you’ll encounter errors that stop development: missing compilers, absent SDK headers, and broken linkers are common symptoms. For example, on Windows Visual Studio's 'Game development with C++' workload installs the MSVC compiler and Windows SDKs Unreal relies on. Without those, a build attempt typically produces errors stating SDK or toolset not found. Why does this matter? C++ gives you deep engine access and performance, but it also directly depends on binary toolchains tied to the OS and SDK versions. A second reason: a consistent environment reduces wasted time. When your engine, compiler, and IDE agree on versions, builds are reproducible across machines and continuous integration. A frequent misconception is that the engine alone is enough; in reality, the IDE and its workloads supply the compilers and linkers that turn source into runnable modules. Takeaway: treat the installation steps as essential, not optional, and verify them by performing a local compile immediately after installation.

keyIdea.title: Toolchain is Essential
keyIdea.text: Unreal Engine plus the correct IDE workloads produce the compilers and SDKs needed for successful C++ builds.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Core Concept
Why the environment matters
  • Toolchains (compiler + SDK) convert C++ to engine modules the OS can run.
  • Missing workloads produce build failures like 'SDK not found' or linker errors.
  • Consistent versions support reproducible builds and easier debugging across machines.
Common misconception
The engine alone isn't enough. You still need the IDE workloads that supply compilers and SDK headers used during compilation.
Concrete example
On Windows, the Visual Studio workloads install MSVC and Windows SDKs. If they are absent, building a simple generated project will fail with missing include or toolset errors.
Check your setup
  1. Open Visual Studio Installer.
  2. Confirm 'Game development with C++' and 'Desktop development with C++' are selected.
  3. Apply changes and retry building the UE5 C++ project.
Key Takeaway

Install both the engine and the correct IDE workloads before writing C++; the build system depends on both.

screens.title: Installing Unreal Engine via Epic Games Launcher
screens.narratorSegment: Installing Unreal Engine through the Epic Games Launcher is the standard first step and is intentionally straightforward, but small choices matter. Start by installing the Epic Games Launcher and signing in. In the Launcher, open the Unreal Engine tab and the Library view. There you'll click the plus icon to add a new engine version and choose the latest stable Unreal Engine 5 release. Download and install that version. After installation, launch the engine to confirm it starts cleanly; this confirms the engine files are present and the Launcher can initialize the editor. A useful practice is to verify the engine version number in the editor's About panel so you can match it to the documentation and online resources. A common mistake is assuming any UE5 build will behave identically; different minor engine versions may change APIs. After confirming the engine launches, the next step is to prepare your IDE. If you stop here and attempt C++ development without the IDE toolchain, you will encounter build-time errors. So treat the launcher installation as the first part of a two-step setup: engine first, toolchain second.

keyIdea.title: Engine Install Checklist
keyIdea.text: Add a UE5 version in the Epic Games Launcher, install it, and confirm the editor opens successfully before moving to IDE setup.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Install Engine
Step-by-step
  1. Install Epic Games Launcher and sign in.
  2. Open Unreal Engine → Library and click the + icon to add a version.
  3. Select the latest stable UE5 release and install it.
  4. Launch the editor to verify the install and check the About panel for version confirmation.
Why version matters
APIs and build behavior can differ between minor engine releases. For reproducible work, note the version used for tutorials and projects.
Quick check
  • Editor opens without missing DLL errors.
  • About panel shows chosen UE5 build.
  • Library lists the installed engine version.
Common mistake
Skipping version checks and later discovering APIs differ from tutorial steps.

screens.title: Installing Visual Studio and Selecting Workloads
screens.narratorSegment: On Windows, Visual Studio is the recommended IDE, and it must include specific workloads to build Unreal Engine C++ projects. When you run the Visual Studio installer, you will see workload options; the two essential ones for UE5 are 'Game development with C++' and 'Desktop development with C++'. These workloads install the MSVC compiler toolset, linkers, and Windows SDKs that the engine depends on. If you omit these, compiling the generated solution typically fails with messages about missing SDKs or toolsets. A useful validation is checking for MSVC v143 build tools and a recent Windows SDK in the installer’s individual components view. Installing these workloads may add significant disk usage, so plan time for the download and installation. A common misconception is that simply installing Visual Studio without workloads is sufficient; it is not. After installation, restart your machine if prompted and then try building the generated. sln. If the build succeeds, your IDE is properly configured. If not, examine the Error List in Visual Studio to identify missing components. Installing Visual Studio and Selecting Workloads means choose 'game development with c++' and 'desktop development with c++' to install compilers, linkers, and windows sdks required by ue5.. In practical terms, choose the exact workloads unreal engine requires. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Select Exact Workloads
keyIdea.text: Choose 'Game development with C++' and 'Desktop development with C++' to install compilers, linkers, and Windows SDKs required by UE5.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Install Visual Studio
Installer choices
  • Select 'Game development with C++' to get MSVC and related gaming toolchain items.
  • Select 'Desktop development with C++' for core C++ libraries and desktop SDKs.
  • Optionally check individual components for MSVC v143 and a recent Windows SDK.
Warning
Omitting workloads is the most common source of build failures for new Windows users.
Validation steps
  1. Install Visual Studio Community.
  2. Choose required workloads and complete installation.
  3. Open the generated solution and attempt a Build → Build Solution.
Quick Tip
If you encounter missing toolset errors, re-run the installer and add MSVC v143 and the Windows SDK from Individual components.

screens.title: Visual Studio (Windows) vs Xcode (macOS)
screens.narratorSegment: Unreal Engine C++ development uses different IDEs per platform, and understanding the practical distinctions helps you choose the correct workflow. On Windows the standard is Visual Studio; on Mac O S it's Xcode. Visual Studio requires explicit workload selection to install MSVC, linkers, and Windows SDKs. Missing those workloads is the primary cause of build errors on Windows. Xcode, installed from the App Store on Mac O S, typically includes the compiler and system SDK required for building UE projects, so Mac O S setup tends to be simpler. However, some project or plugin features may still need specific SDK versions on Mac O S, so check the editor's Output Log if builds fail. Another practical difference is file organization: Visual Studio uses a. sln solution file you open to edit multiple projects, while Xcode uses a project workspace. A common misconception is that Mac O S requires no attention — while Xcode installs core tools, you still must ensure your Xcode version is compatible with your engine build. Ultimately, follow the platform-specific setup steps and validate by compiling the generated project.

keyIdea.text: Windows needs Visual Studio workloads explicitly; macOS relies on Xcode's bundled toolchain. Validate builds on each platform.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › IDE Comparison
Visual Studio (Windows)
  • Requires 'Game development with C++' and 'Desktop development with C++' workloads.
  • Uses .sln solution files to organize source projects.
  • Common errors stem from missing workloads or MSVC versions.
Xcode (macOS)
  • Provided via the App Store and typically installs compiler and SDKs.
  • Uses Xcode projects/workspaces to edit generated code.
  • Still validate Xcode version compatibility with the engine.
Misconception check
Don't assume macOS needs no attention. Xcode provides core tools, but version mismatches can cause build trouble. Always run a test compile.

screens.title: Creating a New C++ Project in Unreal Engine 5
screens.narratorSegment: Creating a new C++ project is the first practical step to writing gameplay code. In the Unreal Editor project browser, select Games and then a template — Blank, First Person, or Third Person. For this lab choose Blank and ensure Project Type is set to C++ (not Blueprint). Name the project MyFirstCPPProject and pick a folder location. The engine will scaffold the project, producing a. uproject file and a Source directory containing basic C++ classes such as your game module header and source files. It will also generate a Visual Studio solution (. sln) on Windows or an Xcode project on Mac O S. Open that solution to load the generated source into your IDE; the Solution Explorer shows the Source folder and the generated module files. A common beginner mistake is choosing Blueprint instead of C++, which generates a different project structure and omits the source code. After creating the project, close the editor and open the solution in your IDE to verify files are present and ready for a build attempt. Creating a New C++ Project in Unreal Engine 5 means selecting c++ during project creation generates .uproject, source files, and a solution/project file you will open in your ide.. In practical terms, generate myfirstcppproject and inspect generated files. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Create Project
Create MyFirstCPPProject
  1. Open Unreal Engine and choose Games → Blank.
  2. Set Project Type to C++ and name it MyFirstCPPProject.
  3. Engine generates .uproject, Source folder, and an IDE solution file.
Concrete example
After generation you should see files like MyFirstCPPProject.h and MyFirstCPPProject.cpp under Source in your IDE's Solution Explorer or Navigator.
Quick file check
  • .uproject exists in project root.
  • Source folder contains module headers and source files.
  • .sln or .xcodeproj is present to open in your IDE.
Misstep to avoid
Selecting Blueprint instead of C++ will not generate IDE source files — you must pick C++ to get the code scaffold.

screens.title: Unreal Editor: Viewport, World Outliner, Details, Content Browser
screens.narratorSegment: Once your project opens in the Unreal Editor, it helps to know where to find the elements you will interact with from code. The Viewport is the primary interactive 3D view where you place and preview actors and levels. The World Outliner lists every actor currently present in the active level; it's how you locate specific objects to select or inspect. The Details panel displays the properties of the currently selected actor or asset; these properties can be exposed to Blueprints and to the editor via UPROPERTY macros in C++. Finally, the Content Browser is where all project assets live: textures, materials, Blueprints, and also references to C++ classes compiled into modules. Your C++ classes appear as code assets in the Source folder and, after compilation, often expose editor-facing counterparts that show up in the Content Browser or as components you can attach to actors. A common confusion for beginners is expecting changes in C++ to immediately appear as editable properties; some changes require recompilation and possibly an editor restart to register new UPROPERTY or UFUNCTION additions. Knowing these panels helps you connect the code you write to the actors and assets you manipulate visually.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.1 › Editor Anatomy
Viewport
Interactive 3D view where you place actors and test gameplay. Use Play to preview behavior driven by your C++ code.
World Outliner & Details
World Outliner lists actors; Details shows properties that UPROPERTY exposes to the editor. Changes here affect live actors in the level.
Content Browser
All assets and references live here. Compiled C++ classes surface as usable components and Blueprintable types after a successful build.
Practical note
After adding UPROPERTY or UFUNCTION macros, recompile and sometimes restart the editor to ensure the editor reflects structural code changes.

screens.title: Opening the Solution and Exploring Generated C++ Files
screens.narratorSegment: When Unreal generates a C++ project it creates a solution file you open in your IDE. On Windows double-click the. sln file to open Visual Studio; on Mac O S open the Xcode project. In Visual Studio's Solution Explorer you will see your project module and source files such as MyFirstCPPProject. h and MyFirstCPPProject. cpp. These files provide the basic module implementation and a game module class you can extend. Use the IDE to open these files, explore their includes and class declarations, and set breakpoints for debugging. A short code walkthrough helps: look for module boilerplate that registers the game module and the primary game-mode class. The IDE also provides build configuration options — Debug, Development, or Shipping — which control compiler optimization and debug symbol generation. Beginners sometimes try to edit files outside the solution or manually move files; instead add new C++ classes using the Editor or the IDE, which ensures the build system recognizes them. Opening the solution and scanning the generated files gives you a reliable starting point to add your own gameplay code. Opening the Solution and Exploring Generated C++ Files means open the solution to inspect generated headers and source files; use the ide to build, debug, and add new classes so the build system tracks them.. In practical terms, use your ide's solution explorer to find module and game files. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Compiling from the Editor and IDE
screens.narratorSegment: Compilation can be performed either from within the Unreal Editor using the Compile button or from your IDE by building the solution. Using the Editor's Compile button is convenient for quick iterations: it triggers a build of the changed modules and attempts to hot reload them into the running editor. Building from Visual Studio or Xcode gives you full control and access to the IDE's build output and debugger. Regardless of where you build, always watch the Output Log in the editor or the Error List in your IDE. Successful builds conclude without errors and produce compiler and linker output indicating that modules were generated. If a build fails, the compiler will report files and line numbers; use those to locate syntax problems or missing includes. Common compilation issues include missing workloads (no compiler), incorrect include paths, syntax errors, or plugin conflicts. When you see errors about missing SDKs or toolsets, re-run the Visual Studio installer to add the required components. If errors are purely code-related, fix the source and rebuild. Building often and inspecting logs will make debugging faster and more predictable.

screens.title: Hot Reloading: Fast Iteration and Its Limits
screens.narratorSegment: Hot reloading is an engine feature that attempts to inject compiled C++ changes into the running editor, enabling faster iteration without a full restart. When you change an implementation in an existing function and click Compile, the engine will recompile the modified module and try to apply it to the running process. This is incredibly useful for small tweaks, testing behavior quickly, and shortening development cycles. However, hot reload has limits. Structural changes like adding new UPROPERTY or UFUNCTION macros, changing class inheritance, or adding new reflected types can require a full editor restart to ensure the reflection system registers the new members correctly. Another limitation is when native memory layouts change; in such cases continuing without restart risks inconsistent state. A common misconception is to assume hot reload always preserves runtime state without side effects; in practice you should still save levels and be prepared to restart the editor when working on class definitions or when the editor reports that a restart is required. Use hot reload for small code edits and prefer a restart after major A P I or class-structure changes.

What hot reload does
It recompiles changed modules and attempts to inject new code into the running editor so you can test smaller changes without restarting.
When to restart
Additions like new UPROPERTY/UFUNCTION, modifying inheritance, or structural layout changes typically require a full restart to be reliable.
Concrete example
Changing the body of a function and recompiling often works via hot reload. Adding a new reflected property usually needs restart to register in the Details panel.
Misconception check
Hot reload is not a substitute for a restart after major changes; treat it as a convenience for small edits only.

screens.title: Troubleshooting Common Setup and Compilation Issues
screens.narratorSegment: Troubleshooting setup and compilation issues is mostly about reading error messages and mapping them to the right component. The earliest and most frequent error for new Windows users is missing toolchains: the compiler or Windows SDK is not installed because the Visual Studio workloads were not selected. The error wording often mentions missing toolsets or SDKs; the remedy is to re-run the Visual Studio installer and add the required workloads or individual components. Another common class of errors is incorrect include paths or syntax mistakes in C++ files; these show up in the compiler output with file names and line numbers and should be fixed directly in the code. Linker errors such as unresolved externals indicate missing libraries or mismatched module declarations. Plugin conflicts sometimes surface after adding third-party modules; if a plugin causes build failures, try disabling it or ensuring it supports your engine version. Always use the Output Log in the editor and the Error List in your IDE — they are the primary diagnostic tools. A practical habit is to read the first error, apply a fix, and rebuild, because subsequent errors often cascade from the initial failure.

Welcome. In this lesson you will build a reliable C++ development environment for Unreal Engine 5 so you can move from concept to compiled gameplay code quickly and with fewer interruptions. We begin by using the Epic Games Launcher to install Unreal Engine, then install and configure an IDE — Visual Studio on Windows or Xcode on Mac O S — with the precise C++ workloads the engine requires. Next you'll create a new C++ project and explore the Unreal Editor layout so you know where your code fits with assets and actors. Finally, we'll cover the compilation workflow, including the editor Compile button and the hot reloading mechanism that speeds iteration, and the common setup mistakes that most beginners encounter. A solid environment removes friction: you won’t lose time to missing SDKs, broken toolchains, or confusing error messages. By the end of this chapter you'll be able to create MyFirstCPPProject, open the generated solution in your IDE, compile successfully, and know how to respond when the engine needs a restart. Keep an eye out for the common-mistake checks as you follow each step.

By the end of this chapter you will have four practical competencies that let you start C++ development with Unreal Engine 5. First, you will successfully install and configure Unreal Engine and the C++ IDE so the toolchain is complete and builds succeed. For example, you'll confirm Visual Studio has the 'Game development with C++' and 'Desktop development with C++' workloads. Second, you will understand why those specific workloads and SDKs matter; you'll be able to explain which components provide compilers, linkers, and Windows SDK headers, and why missing them produces build errors. Third, you will create a new C++ project and navigate the Unreal Editor's core panels so you can place actors, inspect properties, and locate your generated C++ classes. Finally, you'll perform a successful compilation, use the Editor's Compile button and hot reloading for fast iteration, and diagnose common setup and compilation problems using the Output Log and your IDE's error list. Each objective is practical: you will leave with a working project named MyFirstCPPProject and the confidence to troubleshoot the usual setup pitfalls.

First, install the Epic Games Launcher, add Unreal Engine 5 from the Library, and confirm the engine runs. Second, install the IDE: on Windows choose Visual Studio Community and during installation explicitly select the 'Game development with C++' and 'Desktop development with C++' workloads; on Mac O S install Xcode. Third, create a new C++ project named MyFirstCPPProject using the Blank template and ensure you choose C++ rather than Blueprint. Fourth, compile the project from the Editor and watch the Output Log for a clean build. If you see any errors, open the generated solution in your IDE and inspect the Error List to find missing SDKs or syntax issues. These validation steps are small but essential: they turn a theoretical install into a working environment that supports real C++ iteration in UE5.

A correct development environment is the foundation of productive Unreal Engine C++ work. Conceptually, the environment is the combination of Unreal Engine itself, the Epic Games Launcher that manages it, and the C++ toolchain your IDE provides. If any part is missing or misconfigured you’ll encounter errors that stop development: missing compilers, absent SDK headers, and broken linkers are common symptoms. For example, on Windows Visual Studio's 'Game development with C++' workload installs the MSVC compiler and Windows SDKs Unreal relies on. Without those, a build attempt typically produces errors stating SDK or toolset not found. Why does this matter? C++ gives you deep engine access and performance, but it also directly depends on binary toolchains tied to the OS and SDK versions. A second reason: a consistent environment reduces wasted time. When your engine, compiler, and IDE agree on versions, builds are reproducible across machines and continuous integration. A frequent misconception is that the engine alone is enough; in reality, the IDE and its workloads supply the compilers and linkers that turn source into runnable modules. Takeaway: treat the installation steps as essential, not optional, and verify them by performing a local compile immediately after installation.
